body:
Opportunity to create housing on Places of Worship land
The City of Waterloo’s Planning Division is initiating an amendment to the City’s Zoning By-law 2018-050 to provide flexibility in how land is used in future. Through this City-led zoning by-law amendment, 14 Places of Worship are proposed to be rezoned from Residential One (R1) or Residential Four (R4) to Residential Mixed Use - 20 to permit multi-unit residential buildings such as six-storey apartment buildings and stacked townhouses if the property owner chooses to do so.
Freestanding places of worship will continue to be permitted on these properties. The City is creating an opportunity, not obligation, by re-zoning church properties to support housing development.
This amendment is a part of the
Housing Accelerator Fund Initiative 9
.
Locally, there have been a number of places of worship that have undergone redevelopment of their lands (in part or in whole) to renew aging worship spaces and create new housing and community spaces. Some projects have redesigned existing buildings, used parking areas or resulted in newly constructed places of worship in conjunction with new housing.
The amendment also seeks to authorize additional community uses within places of worship which will enable "third spaces" to co-locate on the lands if desired. Third spaces are informal, accessible community gathering spots distinct from home ("first place") and work ("second place"). Third spaces may help congregations diversify their sources of income while maintaining worship and community activities.
The properties under consideration for the amendment include:

A summary of the information panels shared during public engagement events
The information in this section was shared as printed panels with attendees during public engagement events. It has been reformatted to make it easy to view online.
The purpose of the amendment is to consider rezoning 12 Places of Worship from their current zoning of Residential One (R1) or Residential Four (R4) to a zone to permit multi-unit residential buildings.
In addition, the amendment seeks to authorize additional community uses within places of worship which will enable third spaces to co-locate on the lands if desired.
Freestanding places of worship will continue to be permitted on these properties. This Zoning By-law Amendment will provide flexibility in how land is used.
Supportive housing
- Facilities with integrated services to help people experiencing or at risk of homelessness live independently
Community of social housing
- Developed with public funding and owned or operated by government, non-profits or co-operatives
Below market cost rental or ownership
- Private rental or owned units subsidized by the government
Private rental
- Units owned by individuals or corporations charging market rents
A diverse range of housing size, price points, and tenures is needed to support a growing and changing population.
In 2025, the median rent for a vacant two-bedroom apartment was $2,033/month. A household would need to earn approximately $81,320 per year to afford this rent while spending no more than 30% of their income on housing.
A Store Clerk in your neighbourhood
Store clerks help keep local businesses operating and provide essential services to residents. Many work full-time but earn between $33,000 and $44,600 per year.
A Store Clerk in your neighbourhood could reasonably afford a maximum rent of approximately $825 to $1,115/month.
A Personal Support Worker in your neighbourhood
Personal Support Workers (PSWs) provide essential care and support to seniors and individuals with disabilities. Many earn between $39,000 and $55,000 per year. A Personal Support Worker in your neighbourhood could reasonably afford a maximum rent of approximately $975 $1,375/month.
A Registered Nurse in your neighbourhood
Registered Nurses provide critical healthcare services in hospitals, clinics, and long-term care facilities. Typical earnings range from $75,000 to $95,000 per year. A Registered Nurse in your neighbourhood could reasonably afford a maximum rent of approximately $1,875–$2,375/month.
A Teacher in your neighbourhood
Teachers educate and support children and youth while helping build strong communities. Typical earnings range from $50,000 to $105,000 per year. A Teacher in your neighbourhood could reasonably afford a maximum rent of approximately $1,250–$2,625/month.
There are both ownership and rental rate benchmarks based on market costs and income.

Answers to common questions
Does a zoning change require mean that development will happen on these properties?
Who initiated this proposal and why?
Were the owners of the properties asked whether they want to be included in Z-26-09 and rezoned?
How were the places of worship selected for inclusion in Z-26-09?
Is there a city initiative to encourage specific development for daycare facilities and/or seniors' residences on these properties?
Where are the details of the zoning bylaw amendment?
FAQ
Does a zoning change require mean that development will happen on these properties?
No. A zoning change
does not require
a property owner to build anything. It simply gives them the legal right to develop or use the property/building in accordance with the new zoning, if they choose.
Who initiated this proposal and why?
This is a City-initiated process, undertaken as part of the City’s Housing Accelerator Fund work. The City received funding from the Federal Government as part of the Housing Accelerator Fund to accelerate the construction of new housing (including new affordable housing), create greater certainty in the development approvals and building permit processes and to streamline various planning processes.
Were the owners of the properties asked whether they want to be included in Z-26-09 and rezoned?
Correspondence was sent to each landowner in advance of Z-26-09 being brought to Council on June 22 for the Informal Public Meeting.
How were the places of worship selected for inclusion in Z-26-09?
The key criteria used was the size of the property and the current zoning. The sites selected for inclusion are zoned residential R1, R4 or R9 and range from 0.87 acres to 5.82 acres in size.
Is there a city initiative to encourage specific development for daycare facilities and/or seniors' residences on these properties?
No. This zone change application (Z-26-09) may provide the opportunity for property owners to pursue these uses, but there is no specific initiative to encourage it.
Where are the details of the zoning bylaw amendment?
City staff are assessing the properties against a broad set of metrics to determine the appropriateness of expanding permitted land uses. This includes parcel size, surrounding land uses, access to transit, proximity to schools and other community amenities, the transportation and infrastructure network. A draft of the zoning bylaw amendment, as well as the full assessment will be available for review prior to the formal public meeting. It will be available in the packet for the Council meeting, as well as posted on Engage Waterloo.
Will a companion Official Plan amendment accompany Z-26-09, and will it change the designation of sites now shown as Low Rise Residential?
An official plan amendment is not proposed with this project. The low-rise residential designation in the official plan already permits stacked townhouse dwellings and low-rise apartments.
When will Council make a decision on this application and how will nearby residents be notified?
The date of the formal public meeting has yet to be determined. As per the Planning Act and the City’s Official Plan, all landowners within 120 metres of each property will be notified of the formal public meeting via a letter in the mail. The meeting information and the staff report that is presented to Council will also be posted on this Engage page and subscribers to the project page will be notified. Click
Follow
at the top of the project page to be notified.
If Council approves Z-26-09, can residents appeal the decision, and have third-party appeal rights been limited for this kind of amendment?
Residents are not able to appeal the decision to the Ontario Land Tribunal. Only the applicant and /or registered owner, a specified person such as utility providers, or a public body such as a municipality, a local board, a hospital, a ministry, department, board, commission, agency or official of a provincial or federal government or Indigenous communities who, before the by-law was passed, made oral submissions at a public meeting or written submissions to the council, may appeal a decision on a zone change application.
What scale of development could the sites accommodate if they are rezoned as RMU-20 and what new-unit count is projected?
The RMU-20 zoning permits an apartment building, a mixed-use building, a townhouse building, a stacked townhouse building, a triplex building, a long term care facility and an assisted living facility with certain ancillary uses permitted on the ground floor of an apartment building or mixed-use building. At this point, no new unit count has been completed.
If these sites are rezoned to RMU-20, what other public process is required before a building is approved?
If a future development plan complies with all zoning regulations, there will be no further public processes for that development. However, it is common for developments to require further amendments/variances to the zoning regulations due to the unique characteristics of the property which will include opportunity for public input. If amendments/variances are proposed, notices will be provided to nearby property owners.
Landowners may also elect to not undertake any new development.
What public notice and consultation has been carried out for Z-26-09 to date?
The zone change application was presented at the Informal Public Meeting (a City Council meeting) on June 22. The purpose of the informal public meeting was to introduce the proposed amendment to Council and the public, and to obtain the preliminary comments of those affected by the proposed amendment.
In advance of the June 22
nd
meeting, landowners within 120 metres of each property were sent a notice in the mail. Information was also posted here on the project webpage (“Engage Waterloo”). Public consultation on the amendment will continue throughout the summer.
How do you prevent places of worship from selling their land to developers now that it has more development potential?
Places of worship are privately owned and have the same property rights and obligations as other landowners.
Will regular communication and review processes be followed should a place of worship proceed to develop their land?
The City of Waterloo must follow the notice, public meeting, and decision-making requirements of the Planning Act.
How does this support the City's Climate Action Plan?
Community climate work is largely governed by the regional community mitigation plan “TransformWR” and is supported by various other city plans and policies. This proposed zoning by-law amendment reflects Strategy 1.5 of TransformWR: Build compact urban and settlement areas that are efficient for energy, services, infrastructure, and transportation, and make existing and new communities “complete communities”. Complete communities are a neighbourhood-scale area or large site that contains an appropriate mix of employment, local services, and other uses including a range of housing types, shops, personal services, green spaces, schools, recreation, open spaces, and other amenities and community uses/infrastructure, within close proximity to each other such that residents can meet their daily or weekly needs within a reasonably short distance.
